chunks: "Overcharging means pushing a cell above 4. 2 volts, or putting in more charge than the anode can accept. The effects escalate with how far and how long. A little over, say 4.
25 to 4. 3 volts, mostly shortens life: the cathode is stripped of more lithium than is healthy, the structure degrades, and the electrolyte slowly oxidizes.
Go further and several things happen. The electrolyte oxidizes at the cathode surface and produces gas, so the pouch swells.
The graphite anode becomes full, so extra lithium plates out as metal, which is permanent capacity loss and can grow dendrites through the separator.
All the energy being pushed in beyond what the cell can store goes into side reactions, and that is heat. Heat speeds up the reactions, which makes more heat.

If it continues, the separator can melt at around 130 degrees, which creates an internal short, and then the cathode releases oxygen at high temperature and the cell goes into thermal runaway, venting and possibly fire, which is the failure everyone knows.
So prevention is layered: the charger holds 4.
2 volts within about 1 percent and terminates on current and a timer; per-cell monitoring stops it for each cell in a series pack; a protection IC opens a MOSFET at around 4.
25 to 4. 35 volts; and cells have mechanical devices and the pack has a fuse and temperature cutoff.
In a series pack, one cell can overcharge while the total looks right, so balancing and per-cell protection matter."
